newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.
newsitem.headline: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London closed lower on origin selling although roaster price fixing supported the market against an overspill of bearish New York sentiment. At the close, November stood $5 higher at $1,521 after touching a low of $1,505. But all other positions ended weaker, with the second-month January contract down $10 at $1,424. The truck drivers' strike in Colombia is continuing but it is not yet clear whether this has affected coffee shipments. In New York arabica futures ended lower as speculative liquidation and options-related selling dragged the key December contract through the critical 110 cent level by the close.

Traders said the market's failure to rebound after three consecutive weaker closes made buyers more cautious. Moreover, hefty differentials, coupled with the mediocre quality of many available spot beans, kept roasters on the sidelines. However, nearby supplies remain tight and roasters continued to rely on shipments of Brazilian coffee, and to a lesser extent Colombian beans. The premium of Colombian coffee has risen recently, which may have something to do with the truckers' strike. On the other hand only 25 percent of the truckers are actually striking and contingency plans have enabled coffee to be moved. Given tight nearby supplies, it would not come as a surprise if prices would go up again.

COLOMBIA - Transportation Minister Carlos Hernan Lopez threatened to declare the trucker strike illegal unless the Colombian Truck Drivers Association agreed to end the action, which has halted all shipments of coffee and other key commodities to Colombia's ports. It was not immediately clear what the government would achieve by outlawing the strike and union sources said drivers were determined to continue pressing their demands, the most important of which is a call for higher shipping rates, which it is hoped, would translate into better wages for truckers. However, Lopez argued that the government's hands are tied as shipping rates are set by individual transportation companies and the laws of supply and demand and not by state regulators.

CUBA - Hurricane Lili could damage the Cuban coffee crop originally expected to be above last year's 250,000 60-kg bags. Hurricane alerts and heavy rains across Cuba have reportedly interrupted harvesting operations. Moreover it is feared, that after the storms tens of thousands of pounds of beans could be rotting on the ground. However, it is too early to quantify any damage and past experience shows that weather calamities are often overrated.

JAPAN - Japan imported 519,179 bags of coffee in August 1996, nearly 4 percent more than was imported the same month the previous year. That brought total imports since the beginning of 1996 up to 3.695 million bags, 1.1 percent less than was imported the same period in 1995. Total imports in calendar year 1995 dropped by nearly 12 percent to 5.324 million bags. Main suppliers of green coffee in January/August 1996 were Brazil (614,000 vs 830,100 bags), Colombia (786,100 vs 659,500 bags) and Indonesia (631,500 vs 507,900 bags).
